newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Five million N.Koreans near starvation.
newsitem.headline: Five million N.Koreans near starvation.

text.p: More than five million North Koreans are near starvation and could die in the next few months unless food arrives, an official of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said on Friday.

Ole Gronning, IFRC's representative in the hardline communist country's capital Pyongyang, said that based on U.N. estimates of the coming harvest in October, the food deficit was expected to be worse in 1998 than in 1997.

While North Koreans live on grassroots and bark, 15,000 tonnes of maize donated by South Korea sits in Dandong, China which lacks enough rail wagons to cope with the amounts, according to IFRC officials.

"We think that a bit more than five million people are in such a bad situation that they will die shortly if they don't get food now and also medical assistance," Gronning told a news conference in Geneva.
"Now we are talking about a famine in the making. We have more than five million people at the level of starvation."
He was speaking after the Federation held a two-day meeting to launch its latest emergency appeal of $18 million to increase its food aid and start medical assistance to North Korea.
The Federation plans to quintuple the number of food aid recipients to 740,000 from the current 139,000, distributing 10,000 tonnes of food a month in daily rations of 450 grams.

No firm pledges were announced by the 14 donor national Red Cross societies who took part, but the Federation was optimistic that donations would be forthcoming, according to Gronning. The head of North Korea's Red Cross, Paek Yong-ho, also attended.
South Korea is already providing corn, rice, wheat flour, soybeans and vegetable oil valued at $11 million under the five-month appeal. "The food component is covered," he said.
The food has been bought by South Korea in China, but nearly 25 trains of maize bound for North Korea are stuck in Dandong, China -- where wagons are lacking, Gronning said.
"Everything now is blocked on the other side of the border because the Chinese railway network is not able to cope with huge amounts of rail movement," he said.
"We are trying to work fast because maize cannot last very long. They also forgot to fumigate it," he added.
The Federation hopes to take the 15,000 tonnes by train to Dailin, China, where it would be put on boats for North Korea.
IFRC has asked South Korea to modify existing contracts and ship the remaining 30,000 tonnes of food via Dailin, China to Nampu port near Pyongyang. It expects the route to be efficient.
Government foods stocks throughout North Korea are virtually empty, according to Gronning. "People are living on grassroots and bark. I have seen it in hundreds of places.

"I would presume that quite a few people have died over the past few months. Personally I have seen quite a few kids in orphanages and kindergartens whom I don't believe are alive today," added the Dane, who travels regularly to 19 counties.
The Federation's random survey in May of 230 school children under age six found 16 per cent had severe malnutrition.
The IFRC's programme, launched in November 1995 after the first of two successive annual floods initially helped those left homeless and without crops. But needs have grown.
The country's population of 23 million needs about 475,000 tonnes of food a month, but less than half that has been available since November, according to Gronning.
"We are now talking about assisting hungry people in general in the country," he said. "The whole population is in bad shape.
"Those who are really in a bad situation are those in the industrial areas. Since the industrial sector is nearly at a standstill they have nothing to barter with."
As the hospital system has nearly collapsed, the IFRC is to provide medicines and equipment, including first aid kits.
Gronning said the American Red Cross was backing its operation and had just donated medical kits for first aid posts.
"The Americans will probably continue through the American Red Cross, at least for the time being," he added.
Mark Preslan, of the American Red Cross, told Reuters: "We came to get detailed information and find out what was not covered. The need is there in all categories."
Kiyoshi Igarashi, of Japan's Red Cross, told Reuters: "The meeting was very informative. We have indicated our interest to support the appeal."
